title: Personal Track Safety
description: Learn essential railway safety procedures, trackside protocols, hazard identification, and emergency responses required for Personal Track Safety certification. This comprehensive module covers all aspects of working safely on and around railway infrastructure.

knowledgeUnits.concept: What defines being 'on or near the line'?
knowledgeUnits.definition: You are on the line itself or within 3 meters (10 foot) of the running line and there are no fences or permanent structures between you and the running line.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Being within 5 meters of the running line with fences between you and the line
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Being anywhere between the boundary fences regardless of distance from the track
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Being on the platform edge when a train is approaching
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Being 'on or near the line' means being on the line itself or within 3 meters (10 feet) of the running line and there are no fences or permanent structures between you and the running line.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Person standing near railway tracks with 3-meter distance marked

knowledgeUnits.concept: What defines being 'on the line side'?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Within the boundary fence and the point that is 'on or near the line' and can be seen by approaching drivers.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Only when standing directly beside the track
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: The area beyond the boundary fence but within sight of the railway
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Only when working on the tracks themselves
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Being 'on the line side' means being within the boundary fence and the point that is 'on or near the line', in a position where you can be seen by approaching train drivers.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of the lineside area within boundary fence

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is a 'position of safety'?
knowledgeUnits.definition: When you are at least the minimum required distance away from the passing train at the maximum line speed it is permitted to travel.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Any location outside the tracks
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Only in designated safety refuges
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Standing in the middle of the 6 foot area between tracks
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A 'position of safety' is a location where you are at least the minimum required distance away from the passing train, based on the maximum speed trains can travel on that line.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Person standing at safe distance from tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the '4 foot' area?
knowledgeUnits.definition: The running line itself.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: The distance between two running lines
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: A position of safety 4 feet from the nearest rail
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: The area between the boundary fence and the running line
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The '4 foot' area refers to the running line itself - the area between the rails where trains run.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of the 4 foot area on railway tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the '6 foot' area?
knowledgeUnits.definition: The space between the 2 running lines.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: A position of safety 6 feet from the nearest rail
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: The area between the boundary fence and the running line
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: The space directly above the tracks up to 6 feet high
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The '6 foot' area is the space between two adjacent running lines (two sets of tracks).
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of the 6 foot area between railway tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the '10 foot' area?
knowledgeUnits.definition: The space between 2 sets of running lines.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: A position of safety 10 feet from the nearest rail
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: The minimum safe distance from high-speed trains
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: The space directly above the tracks up to 10 feet high
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The '10 foot' area refers to the space between two sets of running lines (typically a wider separation than the '6 foot').
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of the 10 foot area between two sets of tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the 'cess' area?
knowledgeUnits.definition: The space between the running line and the boundary fence.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: The drainage area alongside tracks
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: A designated emergency refuge
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: The area beneath the tracks where cables run
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The 'cess' area is the space between the running line (tracks) and the boundary fence. This is often where workers position themselves for safety when trains approach.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of the cess area beside railway tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What are the additional risks of reversible and SIMBIDS lines?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Trains can be signalled to approach from any direction.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: They always operate at higher speeds than normal lines
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: They have less reliable signaling systems
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: They always have third rail electrification
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Reversible and SIMBIDS lines present additional risks because trains can be signaled to approach from either direction, making it essential to maintain vigilance in all directions.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Diagram showing trains approaching from multiple directions

knowledgeUnits.concept: When are you permitted to be on or near the line?
knowledgeUnits.definition: If it is part of your duty with signaller's permission, to inspect your train for faults or damage, to lay emergency protection, or when laying assistance protection during a controlled or emergency evacuation.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Whenever you have completed basic safety training
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Only during daylight hours and good visibility
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Only when trains are not scheduled to run
knowledgeUnits.explanation: You are permitted to be on or near the line only if it's part of your duty with signaller's permission, to inspect a train for faults/damage, to lay emergency protection, or when assisting during a controlled/emergency evacuation.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Railway worker with proper safety equipment on tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What should you consider before going on or near the line?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Line speeds, direction trains normally approach from, and areas of limited clearance.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Only the time of day and weather conditions
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Only if you have high-visibility clothing
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Just the train schedule for that day
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Before going on or near the line, you should consider line speeds (how fast trains travel), the direction trains normally approach from, and any areas of limited clearance where safety positions may be restricted.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Railway worker checking safety information before track access

knowledgeUnits.concept: What protective equipment do you need when on or near the line?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Clean high visibility clothing, safety footwear, and hand lamp.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Just a high-visibility vest is sufficient
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Only a radio communication device
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Standard work clothes and boots
knowledgeUnits.explanation: When on or near the line, you must wear clean high-visibility clothing (so you can be easily seen), safety footwear (to protect against hazards and provide stability), and carry a hand lamp (for visibility in low light or to signal if needed).
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Complete set of required protective equipment for track work

knowledgeUnits.concept: What must you NOT wear when on or near the line?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Anything that would affect your vision or ability to hear approaching trains.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Only loose clothing that could get caught
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Any dark-colored clothing
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Only steel-toed boots are prohibited
knowledgeUnits.explanation: When on or near the line, you must not wear anything that would impair your vision or hearing, as these senses are critical for detecting approaching trains and maintaining situational awareness for safety.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Examples of prohibited items that impair awareness on tracks

knowledgeUnits.concept: What does the acronym MAPS stand for when a train approaches?
knowledgeUnits.definition:
M - Move to a position of safety
A - Acknowledge approaching train
P - Place any tools down on the floor
S - Stay in a position of safety until train has passed and you are sure no other trains are approaching
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: M - Mark the train approach, A - Alert others, P - Prepare to move, S - Signal when clear
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: M - Monitor the approach, A - Assess the speed, P - Protect your position, S - Secure all equipment
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: M - Move safely, A - Approach the cess, P - Position yourself, S - Stand clear of the train
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The MAPS procedure is essential for safety when a train approaches: Move to a position of safety, Acknowledge the approaching train, Place any tools down, and Stay in the position of safety until the train has passed and no others are approaching.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of MAPS protocol with worker responding to train

knowledgeUnits.concept: What must you do if caught between adjacent lines when a train approaches?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Lay face down in the 6 foot, 10 foot or CESS (NOT IN THE 4 FOOT), gather any loose clothing underneath you, do not move until train has passed and you are sure no other trains are approaching.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Run along the track until you find a position of safety
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Lay face down in the 4 foot area until the train passes
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Wave to alert the driver to stop the train
knowledgeUnits.explanation: If caught between adjacent lines when a train approaches, you must lay face down in the 6 foot, 10 foot, or CESS (NEVER in the 4 foot running line), gather loose clothing underneath you, and stay completely still until the train passes and you're sure no other trains are approaching.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration of proper position if caught between lines

knowledgeUnits.concept: What does a red and white squares sign with 'warning limited clearance' indicate?
knowledgeUnits.definition: No position of safety for the length of this structure. You must not attempt to pass while a train is approaching.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: No position of safety, but there are refuges on the opposite side of the railway line
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Reduced speed limit in operation for this section
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Warning of electrical hazards in this area
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A red and white squares sign with 'warning limited clearance' indicates there is no position of safety for the entire length of this structure, and you must not attempt to pass this area while a train is approaching.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Red and white limited clearance warning sign

knowledgeUnits.concept: What does a blue and white square sign with 'warning no refuges' indicate?
knowledgeUnits.definition: No position of safety for the length of this structure. However, there ARE positions of safety or refuges ON OPPOSITE SIDE OF RAILWAY LINE.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: No position of safety in any direction for the length of this structure
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: No protection for workers in this area
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: No train services operating in this section
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A blue and white squares sign with 'warning no refuges' means there is no position of safety for the length of this structure; however, there ARE positions of safety or refuges ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE OF THE RAILWAY LINE.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Blue and white no refuges warning sign

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the role of a COSS?
knowledgeUnits.definition: A COSS is a Controller of Site Safety. They will set up a safe system of work and are there to ensure everyone's safety.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: They are only responsible for managing train movement schedules
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: They only monitor weather conditions for safety impacts
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: They only inspect protective equipment before work starts
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A COSS (Controller of Site Safety) establishes a safe system of work for railway operations, ensuring compliance with safety protocols and protecting all workers at the site.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: COSS supervising work on railway

knowledgeUnits.concept: How do you identify a COSS?
knowledgeUnits.definition: By their BLUE ARMBAND with COSS written in WHITE LETTERS.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: By their white armband with blue lettering
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: By their red armband with white lettering
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: By their yellow high-visibility vest with COSS on the back
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A Controller of Site Safety (COSS) is identified by their BLUE ARMBAND with COSS written in WHITE LETTERS, making them easily recognizable on site.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: COSS with blue armband

knowledgeUnits.concept: How do you identify a Lookout?
knowledgeUnits.definition: By their WHITE ARMBAND with LOOKOUT written in RED LETTERS.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: By their blue armband with white lettering
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: By their yellow armband with black lettering
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: By their orange high-visibility vest with LOOKOUT on the back
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A Lookout is identified by their WHITE ARMBAND with LOOKOUT written in RED LETTERS. Lookouts are responsible for watching for approaching trains and warning workers.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Lookout with white and red armband

knowledgeUnits.concept: How do you identify a Site Warden?
knowledgeUnits.definition: By their WHITE ARMBAND with SITE WARDEN written in BLUE LETTERS.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: By their blue armband with site warden in red letters
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: By their yellow armband with black lettering
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: By their green high-visibility vest with SITE WARDEN on the back
knowledgeUnits.explanation: A Site Warden is identified by their WHITE ARMBAND with SITE WARDEN written in BLUE LETTERS. Site Wardens act as a human barrier between workers and running lines in a 'Separated' green zone arrangement.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Site Warden with white and blue armband

knowledgeUnits.concept: What are the principles of Red Zone working?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Trains are still running. COSS will appoint a 'Lookout' to watch for trains approaching the work area. The 'Lookout' is identified by a white armband with red lettering and carries a blue and white chequered flag and horn.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: All train movements are stopped in the area
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Work is conducted only at night when fewer trains run
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Only emergency or urgent work is permitted
knowledgeUnits.explanation: In Red Zone working, trains continue to run on the lines where work is taking place. The COSS appoints Lookouts who warn workers of approaching trains, allowing them to reach positions of safety before trains arrive.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Red Zone working setup with lookout

knowledgeUnits.concept: What are the principles of Green Zone working?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Green Zone working has three types: Safeguarded (all lines blocked), Fenced (barrier between workforce and running line), and Separated (human barrier/Site Warden between workforce and running line).
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Work is only done during daylight hours when visibility is good
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Only environmental conservation work is permitted
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Work is conducted with reduced speed limits for trains
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Green Zone working provides safer working conditions through three methods: Safeguarded (blocking all train movements), Fenced (physical barriers between workers and active lines), or Separated (Site Wardens acting as human barriers ensuring workers maintain safe distances).
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Green Zone working setup illustration

knowledgeUnits.concept: What are the requirements for a rigid fence in Green Zone working?
knowledgeUnits.definition: For 0-100 mph: 1.25 meters (4 foot) from nearest running line. For 101-125 mph: 2 meters (6 foot 6in). For over 125 mph: no safe distance is possible.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Fences must be at least 3 meters from all tracks regardless of speed
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: All fencing must be electrically grounded regardless of distance
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Only concrete barriers can be used for trains traveling over 75 mph
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Rigid fencing in Green Zone working must be placed specific distances from the nearest running line based on train speeds: 1.25m for 0-100mph, 2m for 101-125mph, and for speeds over 125mph, no fence distance is considered safe.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Rigid fencing with distances marked

knowledgeUnits.concept: What are the requirements for tape fencing in Green Zone working?
knowledgeUnits.definition: For 0-40 mph: 1.25 meters (4 foot) from nearest running line. For 41-125 mph: 2 meters (6 foot 6in). For over 125 mph: no safe distance is possible.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Tape fencing can only be used for speeds under 30 mph
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: All tape must be high-visibility orange regardless of distance
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Tape fencing must always be at least 3 meters from all tracks
knowledgeUnits.explanation: Tape fencing in Green Zone working has different distance requirements than rigid fencing: 1.25m from the nearest running line for trains 0-40mph, 2m for 41-125mph, and no tape fencing is permitted for lines with speeds over 125mph.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Tape fencing with distances marked

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the minimum safe distance that must be maintained from the OHL?
knowledgeUnits.definition: 2.75 meters (9 foot)
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: 1.25 meters (4 feet)
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: 2 meters (6 feet 6 inches)
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: 3.25 meters (10 feet 6 inches)
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The minimum safe distance that must be maintained from the Overhead Line Equipment (OHL) is 2.75 meters (9 feet). This is critical due to the 25,000 volts AC carried by the OHL system.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Illustration showing 2.75 meter distance from OHL

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the voltage of the OHLE?
knowledgeUnits.definition: 25,000 volts AC
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: 750 volts DC
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: 11,000 volts AC
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: 33,000 volts AC
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The OHLE (Overhead Line Equipment) carries 25,000 volts AC and must be considered live at all times, posing a serious electrocution hazard.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: OHL warning sign showing voltage

knowledgeUnits.concept: When crossing railway lines, what is the correct technique?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Cross at 90 degrees, walking ballast to ballast, avoiding stepping on sleepers, rails, and points
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Cross diagonally to minimize time spent on the track
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Cross at 90 degrees, stepping on the rails for stability
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Cross running from ballast to ballast to minimize time spent on the track
knowledgeUnits.explanation: To safely cross a line, cross at a 90-degree angle (perpendicular to the tracks), walk from ballast to ballast, and avoid stepping on sleepers, rails, and points for maximum stability and safety.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Proper track crossing technique

knowledgeUnits.concept: Which is NOT one of the 4 hand signals you could use to stop a train in an emergency?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Both arms extended horizontally to the sides
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Red flag
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Red light
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Any light waved vigorously
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The 4 hand signals you could use to stop a train in an emergency are: Red flag, Red light, Any light waved vigorously, and Two arms raised straight up in the air. Extending arms horizontally is not one of these signals.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Emergency hand signals to stop train

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the location for the ECO and what is the number?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Romford. Internal number 175, external 01708 743545.
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: London Bridge. Internal 999, external 0207 940 6853.
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Liverpool Street. Internal 247, external 01245 782390.
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Clapham Junction. Internal 321, external 01708 382755.
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The Electrical Control Operator (ECO) is located at Romford. For internal communications, use number 175. For external communications, call 01708 743545.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: ECO contact information display

knowledgeUnits.concept: What is the purpose of the orange CANT line at cab roof height?
knowledgeUnits.definition: Indicates you cannot go above this line if OHL are still live
knowledgeUnits.distractor1: Indicates the maximum loading gauge for freight
knowledgeUnits.distractor2: Shows the maximum height of the pantograph
knowledgeUnits.distractor3: Marks the boundary between different electrification zones
knowledgeUnits.explanation: The orange line at cab roof height is the CANT line - it indicates the safety boundary above which you cannot go if the Overhead Line Equipment (OHL) is still live due to electrocution risk.
knowledgeUnits.imageAlt: Orange CANT line on train cab roof
